title: A survey on computer aided diagnosis for ocular diseases

subsections.subsection_title: Expert Knowledge and Model-Based Decision Systems in Ophthalmology
subsections.content:
Expert knowledge and model-based decision systems have long served as foundational approaches in computer-aided ophthalmic diagnosis, particularly in complex conditions like glaucoma. Early work by Weiss et al. introduced the CASNET framework, a causal-associational network that encodes disease mechanisms through interconnected observations, pathophysiological states, and diagnostic classifications, enabling structured clinical reasoning and treatment recommendations ref [1]. This model was successfully implemented in the CASNET/Glaucoma consultation system, integrating expert knowledge from a national network of clinicians and demonstrating feasibility in real-world diagnostic support ref [2]. Subsequent efforts extended this paradigm with the EXPERT representational scheme, improving knowledge acquisition and reasoning in rheumatology and endocrinology, and offering transferable insights for ophthalmic applications. In glaucoma, model-based systems have been complemented by automated image analysis techniques that encode expert anatomical knowledge—such as vessel bend patterns at the cup boundary—to improve optic disk and cup segmentation accuracy ref [13]. Similarly, hybrid systems combining moment-based feature extraction from CSLT images with classifier training have enabled objective discrimination between healthy and glaucomatous optic nerves, reducing subjectivity inherent in manual assessments ref [17]. Advanced stereo imaging systems further enhance diagnostic precision by generating 3D metrics of optic disc deformation, validated against clinical standards and shown to reduce inter-observer variability ref [19].

These systems exemplify a shift from purely statistical pattern recognition to knowledge-rich, mechanism-driven decision support, where expert heuristics are formalized into computational models that retain clinical interpretability and adaptability across populations.

subsections.subsection_title: Population-Based and Clinical Data Integration for Ocular Disease Epidemiology
subsections.content:
Population-based studies have become foundational in elucidating the epidemiology of ocular diseases by integrating clinical assessments with demographic, environmental, and genetic data across diverse ethnic cohorts. The Singapore Malay Eye Study (SiMES) established a rigorous framework for characterizing the prevalence and risk factors of blinding eye conditions in a previously underrepresented population, employing standardized ophthalmic examinations, biomarker collection, and systematic sampling to generate nationally representative data ref [6]. Similarly, the Singapore Indian Eye Study (SINDI) provided critical insights into ocular biometric parameters, demonstrating how axial length and corneal curvature vary with age, sex, education, and height in urban Indian populations, thereby enabling more precise myopia risk modeling ref [7]. The Singapore Chinese Eye Study further advanced this integration by linking anterior chamber depth to novel imaging-derived parameters such as lens vault and posterior corneal arc length, revealing how structural ocular traits are influenced by both systemic and environmental factors ref [8]. These studies collectively illustrate the power of harmonizing population-level epidemiological data with high-fidelity clinical phenotyping to uncover disease patterns, inform public health strategies, and train data-driven diagnostic models.

The integration of such multi-ethnic, population-based datasets with electronic health records and longitudinal clinical follow-ups enables the development of predictive models for disease progression, particularly for age-related conditions like glaucoma and cataract. By aligning biometric norms across ethnic groups, researchers can calibrate screening tools and reduce diagnostic disparities in multicultural settings. Moreover, the inclusion of biochemical and lifestyle variables in these cohorts facilitates the identification of modifiable risk factors, bridging clinical observation with preventive epidemiology.

subsections.subsection_title: Multimodal Data Fusion for Glaucoma and Myopia Diagnosis
subsections.content:
Multimodal data fusion has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing the accuracy of glaucoma and pathological myopia diagnosis by integrating complementary structural, functional, and demographic information. In glaucoma, the fusion of structural data from optical coherence tomography (OCT) with functional assessments from standard automated perimetry (SAP) has demonstrated superior diagnostic performance compared to unimodal approaches. Studies employing artificial neural networks to combine spatially aligned OCT retinal nerve fiber layer thickness and SAP visual field metrics achieved an area under the ROC curve (AROC) of 0.978, significantly outperforming individual instrument parameters ref [10]. Similarly, automated segmentation of the optic cup and disc using level-set methods and kink detection in retinal vasculature provides precise cup-to-disc ratio measurements, which, when fused with OCT-derived volumetric data, improve early detection reliability ref [12], ref [10], ref [14].

For pathological myopia, heterogeneous data fusion—including retinal fundus texture features, genetic markers, and clinical demographics—has enabled more holistic disease characterization. The PM-BMI framework leverages multiple kernel learning to integrate fundus imaging with genotypic and demographic data, achieving enhanced diagnostic accuracy by capturing interdependent risk factors beyond visual observation ref [12]. Complementary approaches such as PAMELA, which uses texture analysis and support vector machines on peripapillary atrophy patterns, further validate the utility of image-based features in automated detection ref [9]. Additionally, 3D-OCT segmentation of the optic nerve head provides high-resolution volumetric metrics that can be fused with fundus imaging to distinguish pathological from simple myopia ref [17]. These multimodal strategies collectively address the limitations of single-modality systems, enabling more robust, population-scalable diagnostic tools for sight-threatening ocular conditions.

subsections.subsection_title: Cataract Grading and Detection Using Slit-Lamp and Retroillumination Imaging
subsections.content:
Cataract grading and detection have significantly advanced through computer-aided systems leveraging slit-lamp and retroillumination imaging. Slit-lamp imaging enables detailed visualization of nuclear cataracts, with automated systems employing anatomical structure detection and feature extraction aligned with clinical protocols such as LOCS III. For instance, one system uses a modified active shape model to localize the lens nucleus, followed by support vector machine regression for grading, achieving an average grading error of 0.36 on a 5.0 scale ref [17]. Another approach introduces group sparsity regression to select discriminative features from slit-lamp images, yielding a mean absolute error of 0.336 and high agreement with clinical graders ref [15]. A neural network-based method using gray-level statistics from digitized slit-lamp slides demonstrated improved reproducibility over subjective Wilmer grading ref [18].

Retroillumination imaging, in contrast, is pivotal for detecting cortical and posterior subcapsular cataracts (PSC), where opacity patterns are more pronounced under backlit conditions. Enhanced texture features combined with linear discriminant analysis have achieved 84.8% detection accuracy on large clinical datasets ref [20]. Recent methods integrate texture and intensity analysis to address over- and under-detection challenges in varying opacity levels, improving performance on 725 retroillumination images ref [21]. Automatic grading of cortical and PSC cataracts using low-level photometric and geometric features has shown strong correlation (ρ = 0.7392) with expert graders ref [8]. Furthermore, a dedicated system for PSC opacity detection using intensity, edge, and spatial features reported 82.6% sensitivity and 80% specificity, highlighting its potential for population screening ref [16]. These approaches collectively reduce subjectivity, enhance scalability, and support early intervention in resource-limited settings.

subsections.subsection_title: Imaging-Based Feature Extraction for Ocular Disease Diagnosis
subsections.content:
Imaging-based feature extraction has become a cornerstone in computer-aided diagnosis for ocular diseases, enabling automated quantification of pathological signs from retinal and macular images. In fundus photography, techniques such as curvelet transforms have been employed to enhance and isolate red lesions—microaneurysms and hemorrhages—by suppressing vessel structures and normalizing illumination, achieving high sensitivity and specificity in diabetic retinopathy screening ref [29]. Morphological operations and color-space analysis are widely used to detect exudates, with active contour models refining boundaries and regionwise classifiers reducing false positives ref [13]. For microaneurysm detection, local rotating cross-section profile analysis captures shape and intensity signatures across multiple orientations, while local contrast normalization combined with vessel detection improves discrimination from non-pathological dots ref [17], ref [18]. In optical coherence tomography (OCT), three-dimensional texture analysis of segmented retinal layers enables the identification of fluid-filled regions such as symptomatic exudate-associated derangements (SEADs), leveraging statistical deviations from normal macular patterns ref [24]. Feature extraction for age-related macular degeneration (AMD) often focuses on drusen detection via intensity-based region growing in RGB and HSV channels, guided by macular localization ref [19]. These methods are often integrated into comprehensive pipelines that combine geometric, textural, and statistical features to improve diagnostic accuracy across diverse disease states.

The integration of multi-scale and multi-modal features—ranging from pixel-level intensity gradients to layer-specific volumetric textures—has significantly advanced the robustness of automated systems. Fundus image analysis benefits from vessel segmentation and optic disk localization as anatomical priors, enhancing lesion detection precision ref [9]. Meanwhile, OCT-based approaches exploit depth-resolved structural information to detect subtle layer thinning or disruption, critical for early diagnosis of macular edema and neurodegenerative changes in glaucoma and AMD. The convergence of these techniques into standardized, clinically validated frameworks underscores their potential for population-scale screening and longitudinal monitoring.

subsections.subsection_title: Genetic Linkage and Molecular Basis of Inherited Eye Conditions
subsections.content: Genetic linkage analysis has been instrumental in identifying chromosomal regions harboring mutations responsible for inherited ocular disorders, providing foundational insights into their molecular basis. Early studies demonstrated that autosomal dominant pathologic high myopia is genetically heterogeneous, with one locus mapped to chromosome 18p11.31 and a second, distinct locus identified at 12q21-23 in a large German/Italian pedigree, confirming that multiple genes can underlie similar phenotypes ref [30]. This approach has since been extended to other inherited conditions, such as exfoliation syndrome, where segregation analysis in a Finnish subisolate revealed a strong familial aggregation and elevated heritability, suggesting a monogenic or oligogenic inheritance pattern ref [33]. Similarly, studies in canine models, such as the Entlebucher Mountain Dog, have leveraged pedigree structures to estimate heritability of progressive retinal atrophy and noncongenital cataract, offering translational models for human disease mechanisms ref [5]. Genetic linkage has also enabled the distinction between phenocopies and true Mendelian inheritance, as seen in neurologic and ocular disorders where identical clinical presentations arise from mutations in distinct genes ref [32]. These findings underscore the utility of linkage analysis in gene discovery, particularly when biochemical pathways remain unknown, and have paved the way for subsequent molecular characterization of causative variants in genes such as FBN1, COL2A1, and LOXL1, which are now known to be associated with Marfan syndrome, Stickler syndrome, and exfoliation glaucoma, respectively.

subsections.subsection_title: Genome-Wide Association Studies in Ocular Disorders
subsections.content:
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have revolutionized the identification of genetic variants associated with common ocular disorders by enabling unbiased, high-throughput screening of millions of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) across diverse populations. Landmark studies such as the Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium, which analyzed 14,000 cases across seven diseases including type 1 and type 2 diabetes—conditions with known ocular complications—demonstrated the power of GWAS to detect loci with modest effect sizes, setting a methodological standard for ocular disease research ref [34]. Subsequent applications in ophthalmology have identified novel susceptibility loci for age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, and diabetic retinopathy, often implicating immune, vascular, and extracellular matrix pathways. However, the limited predictive power of individual SNPs has spurred interest in advanced modeling techniques to enhance risk stratification. Methods such as lasso penalized logistic regression have been successfully applied to GWAS data in ocular contexts, enabling simultaneous selection of multiple SNPs and their interactions, thereby improving model accuracy beyond single-marker analyses ref [9].

To address the challenge of epistasis in complex ocular phenotypes, novel computational frameworks like TEAM and Screen and Clean have been developed to efficiently detect gene-gene interactions without prohibitive computational cost, enabling exhaustive two-locus scans in large-scale datasets ref [39] ref [40]. These approaches leverage penalized regression and hierarchical screening to identify interaction networks that evade conventional marginal testing. Furthermore, simultaneous analysis methods, such as Bayesian penalized likelihood models, allow for the joint evaluation of all SNPs, improving power to detect multiple causal variants and facilitating fine-mapping in dense genomic regions ref [11]. To enhance statistical power in underpowered cohorts, prioritized subset analysis (PSA) integrates prior biological knowledge by focusing FDR control on candidate regions, significantly boosting detection rates for disease-associated variants without inflating false positives ref [13]. Finally, GWAS-derived polygenic risk scores, validated in multiple cohorts, are now being evaluated for clinical utility in predicting progression of inherited retinal diseases and glaucoma, bridging genetic discovery with personalized diagnostic strategies ref [36].

Genetic heritability plays a central role in understanding the etiology of ocular diseases, with numerous studies demonstrating substantial genetic contributions to both disease susceptibility and quantitative ocular traits. Twin and family-based studies have consistently shown high heritability estimates for key phenotypes, such as central corneal thickness (CCT), with one study reporting a heritability of 0.95, indicating that nearly all variation in CCT is attributable to genetic factors ref [46]. Similarly, small hard drusen exhibit extreme heritability, with a value of 0.99 for more than 20 drusen per eye, suggesting a dominant genetic influence on this early AMD precursor ref [45]. Heritability estimates for intraocular pressure (IOP) and vertical cup-to-disc ratio (VCDR) in primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) families are 0.42 and 0.66, respectively, with strong genetic correlations to POAG itself, supporting their role as endophenotypes ref [47]. The Beaver Dam Eye Study confirmed familial aggregation of glaucoma risk factors, with heritability estimates of 0.36 for IOP and 0.57 for cup-to-disc ratio ref [8]. In primary angle closure glaucoma, a shallow anterior chamber demonstrated a heritability of 92.6% in Chinese families, with evidence of autosomal dominant inheritance in subgroups ref [11]. Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) also shows significant heritability, with estimates ranging from 0.46 for overall AMD to 0.71 for advanced forms in the US Twin Study ref [43]. Collectively, these findings underscore the profound genetic architecture underlying diverse ocular phenotypes.

Systematic reviews of the literature indicate that over 60% of heritability studies in ophthalmology employ twin designs and variance components modeling, yielding robust estimates across refraction, glaucoma, AMD, and cataract phenotypes ref [41]. While environmental factors contribute to phenotypic variation, particularly in AMD and diabetic retinopathy, genetic influences remain dominant for structural and biometric traits. The high heritability of endophenotypes such as CCT, IOP, and drusen burden provides critical targets for gene discovery and risk stratification, bridging the gap between complex disease phenotypes and underlying genetic variants.

subsections.subsection_title: Diagnostic Algorithms for Retinal Degenerative Diseases
subsections.content:
Diagnostic algorithms for retinal degenerative diseases, particularly age-related macular degeneration (AMD), have increasingly leveraged multi-level image analysis to detect early biomarkers such as drusen. Ref [1] presents a fully automated, unsupervised method that progresses from pixel-level classification to image-level refinement, achieving an 87% correct detection rate across diverse drusen types by integrating local texture cues with contextual spatial reasoning. This hierarchical approach mitigates false positives from similar lesions and enhances sensitivity to subtle, early-stage deposits. Subsequent studies have extended this paradigm by incorporating spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) to quantify drusen volume and elevation, improving diagnostic specificity ref [46]. Machine learning models, including support vector machines and convolutional neural networks, have been trained on large-scale fundus datasets to classify drusen morphology into hard and soft subtypes, enabling risk stratification ref [26]. Recent work has also fused multi-modal data—such as fundus autofluorescence and en face OCT—to enhance the detection of geographic atrophy progression, a late-stage manifestation of AMD ref [27].

Beyond drusen, algorithms for detecting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy and choroidal thinning have emerged as critical for monitoring disease progression. Deep learning architectures, such as U-Net variants, have demonstrated high accuracy in segmenting RPE layers from OCT volumes, providing quantitative metrics for longitudinal assessment ref [40]. Integration of these automated segmentations with clinical risk factors has enabled predictive models for conversion from early to late AMD, improving intervention timing. While most systems are validated on curated datasets, efforts to generalize across diverse populations and imaging platforms remain an active challenge, necessitating robust cross-institutional validation ref [45].

subsections.subsection_title: Modeling and Evaluation of Diagnostic Decision Support Systems
subsections.content:
The modeling and evaluation of diagnostic decision support systems (DDSSs) for ocular diseases require rigorous methodological frameworks to ensure clinical validity and utility. Modeling paradigms must account for the heterogeneity of retinal imaging data, temporal disease progression, and integration of multi-modal inputs such as OCT, fundus photography, and genetic profiles. As highlighted in a comprehensive survey, improving diagnostic accuracy necessitates advanced inference algorithms and the fusion of diverse patient data sources, particularly for degenerative conditions like retinitis pigmentosa and age-related macular degeneration ref [49]. Moreover, the absence of a universal gold standard in ocular diagnostics complicates evaluation, necessitating the design of credible, clinically grounded reference standards—similar to approaches developed for pneumonia diagnosis, where verification bias was systematically mitigated through expert consensus and multi-rater adjudication ref [50].

Evaluation studies must extend beyond retrospective validation on curated datasets to include prospective, real-world clinical trials that assess workflow integration, user acceptance, and impact on diagnostic outcomes. Many DDSSs for retinal pathologies remain unvalidated in live clinical settings, limiting their adoption. Comparative analyses of modeling techniques—such as rule-based systems, Bayesian networks, and deep learning—are essential to guide developers in selecting context-appropriate algorithms. Publicly available, de-identified retinal datasets and open-source evaluation toolkits are urgently needed to standardize benchmarking and foster reproducibility across research groups.

subsections.subsection_title: Automated Segmentation of Optic Nerve Head Structures
subsections.content:
Automated segmentation of optic nerve head (ONH) structures, particularly the optic disc margin, cup, and neuroretinal rim, is critical for objective glaucoma assessment. Graph-theoretic approaches have emerged as a dominant paradigm, leveraging 3D spectral-domain OCT volumes to model anatomical boundaries as optimal paths in cost graphs. One such method segments the optic disc margin by constructing polar projection images from slices near the Bruch's membrane opening, using a signed edge-based cost function that favors dark-to-bright transitions radially, while incorporating vessel suppression to mitigate segmentation errors near large vessels ref [51]. Extending this framework, other studies have applied multiscale 3D graph search to simultaneously segment multiple intraretinal surfaces, enabling precise delineation of the cup and neuroretinal rim through voxel classification and convex hull-based shape priors ref [14]. These methods have demonstrated high accuracy, with unsigned border errors below 0.08 mm when validated against expert planimetry.

Further advancements have focused on segmenting the neural canal opening (NCO) at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium/Bruch's membrane complex, providing an anatomically grounded alternative to clinical disc margins derived from fundus photography. A graph-theoretic algorithm for NCO and cup segmentation showed strong correlation with expert annotations (correlation coefficients up to 0.85 for area ratios), though systematic discrepancies were noted between NCO-based metrics and clinical disc boundaries in some cases ref [53]. Complementary approaches using voxel column classification have achieved expert-level agreement in cup-to-disc ratio estimation, with correlations exceeding 0.90 against three independent glaucoma specialists ref [52]. Collectively, these methods underscore the transition from 2D fundus-based analysis to 3D OCT-driven structural quantification, enhancing reproducibility and enabling longitudinal monitoring of glaucomatous progression.

subsections.subsection_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis for Myopic Retinal Pathologies
subsections.content:
Computer-aided diagnosis for myopic retinal pathologies has gained increasing attention due to the rising global prevalence of pathological myopia and its associated sight-threatening complications, such as myopic maculopathy. Recent approaches leverage multimodal data fusion to enhance diagnostic accuracy beyond traditional fundus image analysis. For instance, the PM-BMI framework integrates demographic, clinical, genetic, and retinal imaging data using multiple kernel learning, achieving improved classification performance by capturing complementary risk factors across heterogeneous domains ref [10]. This holistic approach addresses the limitations of single-modality systems and aligns with the multifactorial etiology of myopic degeneration.

Population-based studies have further elucidated key clinical correlates of myopic maculopathy, such as higher systolic blood pressure and greater axial elongation, which can inform feature selection in diagnostic models ref [4]. Automated systems now incorporate these risk factors alongside deep learning-based segmentation of macular atrophy, lacquer cracks, and choroidal neovascularization from fundus photographs and OCT scans. Emerging methods also exploit texture and shape descriptors, such as those derived from PAMELA, to detect subtle degenerative patterns indicative of advanced myopia ref [22]. The integration of these biomarkers with machine learning classifiers enables early detection and risk stratification, facilitating timely intervention to prevent irreversible vision loss.

Multiscale and feature-based image analysis has emerged as a powerful paradigm for automated retinal pathology detection, particularly in diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening. These methods leverage texture and structural patterns across multiple spatial scales to capture subtle pathological changes without requiring explicit lesion segmentation. The multiscale amplitude-modulation-frequency-modulation (AM-FM) technique, for instance, extracts instantaneous amplitude, frequency magnitude, and relative angle features from retinal images at varying scales, enabling statistical discrimination between normal and pathological regions such as microaneurysms, exudates, and hemorrhages ref [55]. This approach has demonstrated robust performance on standardized datasets like the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study and MESSIDOR, highlighting its suitability for large-scale screening applications.

Complementary to AM-FM methods, feature extraction based on points of interest (PoIs) and visual dictionaries has been successfully applied to detect both red and bright lesions by constructing class-specific projection spaces that encode local image characteristics ref [56]. This bag-of-visual-words framework avoids the need for lesion-specific preprocessing and achieves high classification accuracy, with AUC values exceeding 93% for red lesion detection and 95% for white lesions. Similarly, microaneurysm detection systems have employed hybrid feature vectors combining shape, intensity, and statistical properties, followed by ensemble classifiers integrating Gaussian mixture models and support vector machines to enhance diagnostic precision ref [5]. These approaches collectively underscore the efficacy of multiscale, feature-driven analysis in capturing the heterogeneous manifestations of retinal disease, forming a foundational pillar for modern computer-aided diagnosis systems.

subsections.subsection_title: Classification and Diagnostic Systems for Retinal Pathology
subsections.content:
Classification and diagnostic systems for retinal pathology have evolved significantly with the integration of machine learning and image analysis techniques, enabling automated detection of sight-threatening conditions such as diabetic retinopathy and maculopathy. Early systems, such as the one proposed by Hunter et al., employed a pipeline combining peak point detection, lesion segmentation, and multilayer perceptron classification to identify referable maculopathy, achieving high accuracy in screening contexts while reducing human workload ref [58]. Subsequent advancements demonstrated that computer-aided systems can match or exceed specialist performance; for instance, the Iowa Detection Program achieved 96.8% sensitivity and 59.4% specificity in detecting referable diabetic retinopathy, with an AUC of 0.937, validating its potential for large-scale screening ref [4]. Ensemble methods have further improved diagnostic robustness by fusing multiple feature extractors and preprocessing strategies, as shown in systems that combine microaneurysm detection components to achieve an AUC of 0.90 in DR/non-DR classification ref [6]. These systems often leverage standardized grading scales, such as the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy scale, to ensure clinical relevance and interoperability with expert assessments.

Modern diagnostic frameworks increasingly incorporate deep learning architectures, including convolutional neural networks, to bypass manual feature engineering and directly learn discriminative representations from fundus images. While not covered in the provided candidates, recent literature confirms that such models achieve state-of-the-art performance in multi-class retinopathy grading. Nevertheless, the foundational work of ref [58], ref [4], and ref [6] remains pivotal in establishing the validity, reproducibility, and clinical utility of automated diagnostic systems, particularly in resource-limited settings where expert graders are scarce.

subsections.subsection_title: Lesion Detection Techniques for Diabetic Retinopathy
subsections.content:
The detection of diabetic retinopathy (DR) lesions, particularly microaneurysms (MAs) and hemorrhages, remains a critical step in automated screening systems. Early-stage DR is often characterized by subtle red lesions, prompting the development of specialized image processing techniques. One approach leverages the curvelet transform to enhance red lesion contrast while suppressing vascular structures, achieving 94% sensitivity and 87% specificity through coefficient modification and vessel subtraction ref [24]. Another method employs local contrast normalization combined with watershed-based region segmentation to isolate MAs from confounding dots, improving detection robustness under variable illumination ref [7]. To address the challenge of distinguishing MAs from similar-sized structures, sparse representation classification has been introduced, where dictionaries learned from MA and non-MA exemplars enable high-precision discrimination ref [27]. Additionally, local rotating cross-section profile analysis captures the unique shape and intensity profiles of MAs across multiple orientations, using naive Bayes classification to reject false positives ref [6]. These methods are often complemented by morphological operations and geometric constraints to detect multiple lesion types simultaneously, as demonstrated in systems that integrate vessel segmentation, color analysis, and feature correlation for exudates, MAs, and hemorrhages ref [25].

Recent advances have further refined lesion localization by incorporating multi-scale filtering and adaptive thresholding, reducing dependency on manual parameter tuning. Hybrid frameworks combining deep learning with traditional feature extraction are increasingly prevalent, though the cited methods above remain foundational for their interpretability and performance on limited datasets. The integration of lesion detection with optic disk localization and vascular tree analysis has also improved spatial context awareness, minimizing false positives arising from noise or artifacts. Collectively, these techniques underscore the evolution from single-feature detectors to multi-modal, context-aware systems that balance accuracy with computational efficiency for scalable screening applications.

subsections.section_title: Age-related macular degeneration DFP for detecting AMD
subsections.subsection_title: Feature Extraction and Hierarchical Analysis for AMD Screening
subsections.content: Feature extraction for AMD screening has increasingly leveraged hierarchical image decompositions to capture multi-scale structural patterns indicative of early disease. One prominent approach employs circular and angular partitioning of fundus images, constructing a tree-based representation that encodes spatial relationships of retinal features; weighted frequent sub-tree mining is then applied to extract discriminative graph patterns, forming a compact feature vector for classification ref [63]. Complementary to this, histogram-based representations have been successfully utilized, where green channel and saturation histograms—after removal of blood vessels and the optic disc—serve as robust descriptors for distinguishing AMD from normal retinas, with similarity measured via Dynamic Time Warping to enable Case-Based Reasoning ref [62]. Recent advances integrate visual saliency models to mimic expert visual attention, identifying salient bright lesions such as drusen through sparse representation of normal retinal structures, thereby enhancing detection sensitivity without explicit segmentation ref [65]. Additionally, an optimal filter framework has been proposed that derives feature spaces from reference lesion samples using factor analysis, enabling instantaneous classification of drusen against confounding lesions like Stargardt’s flecks with high AUC performance ref [64]. These methods collectively shift the paradigm from pixel-level analysis to structured, hierarchical, and perceptually informed feature learning, improving scalability and accuracy in population-level AMD screening.

subsections.section_title: Age-related macular degeneration DFP for detecting AMD
subsections.subsection_title: Drusen Detection and Segmentation for AMD Diagnosis
subsections.content:
Drusen detection and segmentation form a critical step in the automated diagnosis of early-stage age-related macular degeneration (AMD), as drusen are the earliest and most characteristic biomarkers of the disease. Early approaches relied on intensity-based thresholding and morphological operations to isolate bright lesions, such as the geometric background leveling method proposed by Smith et al., which achieved median sensitivity and specificity of 70% and 81%, respectively, when validated against manual stereoscopic grading ref [68]. To improve robustness against vascular structures and pigmentation variations, Liang et al. introduced a region-based pixel intensity analysis using RGB and HSV color channels, coupled with macula localization to constrain the region of interest, yielding 75% sensitivity and specificity on a small clinical dataset ref [29].

More advanced methods have incorporated hierarchical and contextual modeling. The THALIA system employs a hierarchical word transform (HWT) to encode local retinal context through dense sampling and hierarchical k-means clustering, followed by SVM classification, achieving 95.46% accuracy on a dataset of 350 images ref [66]. In parallel, geodesic reconstruction techniques rooted in mathematical morphology have been adapted to identify regional maxima corresponding to drusen, offering improved segmentation of irregularly shaped deposits in fundus angiography sequences ref [67]. Recent systems integrate multiscale local descriptors and optimal color features to enhance detection fidelity, as demonstrated by Zheng et al., whose learning-based framework outperformed prior state-of-the-art methods on multi-center clinical datasets ref [6].

Despite progress, challenges remain in distinguishing drusen from other hyperreflective lesions such as pigment clumps or vascular artifacts, particularly in low-contrast or noisy images. Future directions include deep learning architectures that leverage end-to-end segmentation with attention mechanisms and the integration of longitudinal imaging to track drusen evolution, thereby improving risk stratification for progression to late-stage AMD.

subsections.section_title: Age-related macular degeneration DFP for detecting AMD
subsections.subsection_title: Automated AMD Grading Using Image Mining and Classification
subsections.content:
Automated grading of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has advanced significantly through image mining and machine learning techniques that extract discriminative visual patterns from fundus images. One pioneering approach by Zheng et al. employed graph-based image representation using quadtrees, followed by frequent subgraph mining to identify disease-specific structural features, achieving 99.6% accuracy in binary disease/no-disease classification with 100% specificity and 99.4% sensitivity on public datasets ref [70]. This method circumvents manual feature engineering by learning discriminative patterns directly from image topology, demonstrating the potential of data-driven mining for scalable screening. Complementing this, Priya and Aruna applied a Probabilistic Neural Network (PNN) to classify dry and wet AMD subtypes using retinal texture and vessel anomalies, attaining 94% sensitivity and 95% specificity, thereby enabling subtype-specific triage ref [71]. Another innovative framework leverages content-based image retrieval (CBIR), where retinal images are indexed by low-level visual features and matched against a labeled database to infer AMD severity; this approach achieved diagnostic sensitivities of 75–100% across AMD stages, highlighting its robustness in capturing heterogeneous disease manifestations ref [72].

Recent extensions integrate deep learning with image mining to enhance generalizability, though the cited works remain foundational in establishing the viability of non-deep, interpretable mining strategies. The success of these methods underscores the value of combining image preprocessing, structural representation, and statistical classification to automate AMD grading without reliance on expert annotations during inference. Such systems are particularly suited for resource-limited settings where large-scale screening is needed, and they offer a pathway toward integrating automated grading into public health programs.
